money.note: Individuals gave $625,403; PAC money $465,498; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Republican U.S. Representative for Alabama's 4th District since January 1997. Attorney with a J.D. from Samford's Cumberland School of Law. Earlier served as Haleyville municipal judge and as a legal aide to Gov. Fob James. Chairs the House Appropriations subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education.

controversies.text: Federal records show $27,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $2,251 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 2 staff trips paid for by that foundation.
Missed 20 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (3.0%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 6, 2026-05-20 to 2026-05-20.

On Dec. 10, 2020, Aderholt backed Texas's Supreme Court lawsuit over the 2020 election and said he had signed a supporting brief. On Jan. 6–7, 2021, he voted to object to Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes. Both objections failed. He said there were "too many reports of serious fraud" for the matter not to be debated.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump (R) is listed as endorsing Aderholt in the 2026 election.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions from Aderholt on data centers, new development or growth limits, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buying, H-1B visas, or school choice and teacher pay. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in 2020, 2022, 2024 or 2026. No page we read covered his positions on red-flag laws, suppressors or gun purchase ages beyond a general campaign statement. Ballotpedia's page was cut off partway through, so later sections were not read. No controversy beyond his January 2021 election-certification votes was found.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: U.S. Representative since 1997 (15 terms) on the House Appropriations Committee, including as a subcommittee chair. Before that he was a practicing attorney, Haleyville municipal judge (appointed 1992), and a legal aide to Gov. Fob James.
qual.why: Nearly three decades in the House with budget oversight work on Appropriations, plus a law degree, legal practice and judicial experience, put him in the top rubric band.
qual.label: Nearly three decades in the House with budget oversight work on Appropriations, plus a law degree, legal practice and judicial experience, put him in the top rubric band.

pro-life.evidence: Said at the January 2010 March for Life that he encourages colleagues to 'look for ways to curb and stop abortions in the United States'; Wikipedia also reports he supported the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade and called it a 'watershed moment for life'.

second-amendment.evidence: His campaign site says he supported expanding gun freedoms relating to the right to carry, has opposed attempts to limit gun rights, and holds an 'A' rating from the NRA.

back-police-order.evidence: His campaign site says he supports police, calls defunding police departments counterproductive, and backs building on current training and hiring programs.

workers-first.evidence: Voted Yea on the Laken Riley Act, which requires DHS to detain certain people in the U.S. without legal permission who are arrested for burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting; it was signed into law on 1/29/2025.

prio.label: Matches 4 of 4 priorities; 1 backed by their record, 3 only promised

roots.summary: Ballotpedia and Wikipedia record his birth in Haleyville, Alabama, and his campaign site says he was raised in Alabama, attended its public schools and lives in Haleyville.

cands.name: Amanda Pusczek

money.note: Individuals gave $22,154; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Registered nurse with over a decade of experience, including hospital, clinic, school and correctional settings and travel nursing during COVID-19 in New York City. Associate degree from Calhoun Community College, bachelor's from Western Governors University. 2026 Democratic nominee for Alabama's 4th District; has not held public office.

endorsements.text: Her Ballotpedia survey lists endorsements from Progressive Voters Network, BAC Balance and Accountability, Citizens Impeachment and For the Future Victory Fund. These are self-reported.
Ballotpedia lists her on Sway voting-group guides, including Tabitha's List and 'Reject AIPAC from City Council to Congress'.

cands.gaps: We found no documented stances from Pusczek on data centers, development or growth, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor ownership of land, H-1B visas, policing, gun policy or school vouchers. We also found no news coverage, controversies or foreign ties. She has held no office, so there is no record of official actions. Ballotpedia and her campaign site disagree on her birthplace (Alabama versus Ferguson, Missouri). The campaign site's article links (ALPolitics.com, Montgomery Advertiser) were only teasers, and we did not read the articles themselves.

local.label: Roots 80: Her campaign biography says she was born in Missouri, moved to Alabama at age six and has called it home since, apart from a few years in Germany; Ballotpedia lists an Alabama birthplace, which conflicts.

score.why: Raised $22.3k, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Registered nurse for over a decade, including travel nursing during the COVID-19 peak in New York City; no elected or governing office held.
qual.why: She has a real career in nursing but no legislative, executive, legal or policy-office experience, and this is her first run for office.
qual.label: She has a real career in nursing but no legislative, executive, legal or policy-office experience, and this is her first run for office.
